# Writing and Debugging Functions {#sec-functions}



To illustrate the problem, consider a teammate who asks for the
30-day event rate at each of the five HF-HOME sites, one number
per site, for a Monday-morning slide. You write a short function
that filters to a site and summarizes the outcome. You loop it over
a vector of site names copied from last week's report, and you
build the slide from whatever comes back. The slide shows
1 number where there should be
5. Four sites print nothing, and nothing in the
console says an error occurred, because nothing errored. The bug is
not in the data, since HF-HOME's canonical site labels are exactly
`"Site A"` through `"Site E"`. The bug is in the casing and
whitespace of four labels copied from a source that writes them
differently. Two further problems hide it. The function returns
nothing at all when a site matches zero rows, and the loop discards
whatever the function returns. Rereading the function more
carefully is unlikely to find the bug. In this chapter we cover the
tools built for this kind of bug. The time to use them is before
the slide ships, not after someone asks why Site D has no number.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first
place. Therefore, if you write the code as cleverly as possible,
you are, by definition, not smart enough to debug it.*

[Brian W. Kernighan and Rob Pike]{.smallcaps}, *The Practice of
Programming* (1999)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Where this chapter sits: functions are written while wrangling and analyzing, and debugging them is the skill that makes both stages trustworthy rather than merely fast.](14b-functions_files/figure-pdf/fig-functions-pipeline-1.pdf){#fig-functions-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). **You'll need.** @sec-wrangling for the `dplyr` verbs this chapter
reuses, @sec-types for the messy site labels in the running

last section connects to. The code uses:

```r

library(purrr)
library(rlang)
```

and calls `tinytest` with its namespace. All three packages are
installed in this book's environment.

**You'll be able to.**

- Write a function with named arguments, defaults, and `...`, and

- Explain what a closure captures and predict what happens when the

## Why write a function at all {#sec-functions-why}

In a general-purpose program, the usual reason to write a function
is reuse. A function called from ten places saves nine copies of
the logic. A one-off data analysis calls almost nothing from ten
places, so that argument seems weak, and it may seem not to apply
at all. A stronger argument is about correction and verification.
A computation written out five times, once per site, gives a bug
five places to hide. It also gives you five places to fix when the
computation changes. A computation written once as a function and
called five times has one place to fix a bug and one place to write
a test. The acronym for this is DRY (don't repeat yourself). It
remains good advice because the alternative multiplies the cost of
being wrong by the number of copies you made before you noticed.

`site_event_rate()` below computes the 30-day event rate for one
HF-HOME site. The randomization table is joined to the outcomes
table once, outside the function, and the filtering happens inside
it:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)

hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
read_hf <- function(file) {
  readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, file),
                  col_types = readr::cols(patient_id = "c",
                                          .default = "?"))
}
hf_rand <- read_hf("randomization.csv")
hf_outcomes <- read_hf("outcomes.csv")
hf_events <- inner_join(hf_rand, hf_outcomes, by = "patient_id")

site_event_rate <- function(data, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  if (nrow(site_data) > 0) {
    summarize(site_data, n = n(),
              event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
  }
}

site_event_rate(hf_events, "Site A")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   700      0.206
```
:::


Later in this chapter the function above turns out to have a bug.
That is deliberate. Because the logic lives in a function, the fix
is one edit in one place, and the five call sites that use it are
fixed along with it. Five copies of the
`filter()`-then-`summarize()` logic, one per site, would need five
correct edits in the same afternoon. There would also be no
mechanical way to confirm that all five were actually changed.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague argues that a function is not worth
writing for code that will run exactly once, on one dataset, and
never again. Under what condition are they right, and how often
does that condition actually hold for an analysis script?

**Answer.** They are right only if the code genuinely runs once,
with no bug ever found in it and no reviewer ever asking for a
variant. For most analyses that condition does not hold. An
exclusion is revised, a reviewer asks for a sensitivity analysis
on a second subgroup, or a bug is found after the fact and must be
fixed everywhere the faulty logic was pasted. 'Runs once' describes
how the script is invoked. It says nothing about how many times its
logic turns out to matter. The same observation motivates testing
an analysis (@sec-testing-why).
:::

### Exercises

1. Below is the same site-level computation written three times,
   once per site, with a copy-paste error in the third copy (it
   filters on `event_30d == 1` instead of computing a rate). Rewrite
   it as one function called three times, and explain why the
   function form makes the error impossible to introduce silently
   in only one call.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
a <- filter(hf_events, site == "Site A")
a <- summarize(a, n = n(), event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
b <- filter(hf_events, site == "Site B")
b <- summarize(b, n = n(), event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
e <- filter(hf_events, site == "Site E")
e <- summarize(e, n = sum(event_30d == 1, na.rm = TRUE))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
site_rate <- function(data, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  summarize(site_data, n = n(),
            event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
}
site_rate(hf_events, "Site A")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   700      0.206
site_rate(hf_events, "Site B")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   571      0.246
site_rate(hf_events, "Site E")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   290      0.213
```
:::


The error in the pasted version (counting events rather than a
rate) is possible only because the third copy has its own body,
which can be edited independently. Once there is one function,
every call shares the same body. A mistake made while editing it
would therefore show up at every call site, not silently at one of
three.
:::

## Anatomy of an R function {#sec-functions-anatomy}

A function definition has four parts: a name to call it by, the
arguments it accepts, a body that computes something from them,
and a value it returns. `site_event_rate` has two arguments, `data`
and `site_name`. Neither has a default, so both must be supplied at
every call. Adding a default makes an argument optional:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
site_event_rate <- function(data = hf_events, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  if (nrow(site_data) > 0) {
    summarize(site_data, n = n(),
              event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
  }
}
site_event_rate(site_name = "Site B")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   571      0.246
```
:::


A default is evaluated lazily. R does not compute `hf_events` when
the function is defined. It does so only when the function is
called, `data` is needed, and no value was supplied for it. Lazy
evaluation also lets a default refer to another argument, as in
`function(data, n = nrow(data))`. Here `n` is computed from
whatever `data` is at call time. A different mechanism, `...`
(dots), collects any number of additional arguments that the
signature does not name, and forwards them. In this way a wrapper
function can pass extra options through to the function it calls,
without naming every one of them in its own signature:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
summarize_outcome <- function(data, ...) {
  summarize(data, event_rate = mean(event_30d, ...))
}
summarize_outcome(hf_events, na.rm = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   event_rate
#>        <dbl>
#> 1      0.224
```
:::


`na.rm = TRUE` is not an argument that `summarize_outcome()` names.
It passes through `...` to `mean()` unchanged. Unfortunately, the
convenience has a cost. A misspelled argument, `na.rn = TRUE`, is
silently absorbed by `...` and forwarded to `mean()`. `mean()` does
not recognize it either, and silently ignores it. No error is
raised at the call where the typo actually is. When a function has
a small, known set of options to expose, name each argument
explicitly rather than catching it in `...`.

**Implicit return.** R returns the value of the last expression
evaluated in the function body. `return()` is needed only to exit
early, before the last line, typically from inside a condition.
`site_event_rate()` above never calls `return()`. Its value is
whatever its final `if` evaluates to. This is why the branch with
no `else` is dangerous. When the condition is false, the `if`
itself evaluates to `NULL`. That `NULL` is what the function
returns, and nothing marks it as a special case.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
is.null(site_event_rate(hf_events, "nonexistent site"))
#> [1] TRUE
```
:::


A function that reaches the end of its body with nothing left to
evaluate also returns `NULL`, invisibly. This is almost never the
intended value. It is one of the most common sources of a `NULL`
that propagates quietly into something downstream. The other
common source is what happened above, a conditional with no
`else`.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**An `if` with no `else` is a `return(NULL)` with no evidence that
you meant to write one.** Write the `else` branch explicitly, even
if it only raises an error or returns `NA`. A silent default then
becomes a choice you can see later, in the function and in a diff.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** `f <- function(x, verbose = FALSE) { if (verbose) print(x); x + 1 }`
is called as `f(5)`. What does it print, and what does it return?

**Answer.** It prints nothing, because `verbose` defaults to
`FALSE` and the `print(x)` branch is skipped. It returns `6`. The
function's value is the value of its last expression, `x + 1`,
whatever the `if` above it did or did not print. The
`if (verbose) print(x)` line is evaluated for its side effect
(printing). Its value, here an invisible `NULL` because `verbose`
is `FALSE`, is discarded, since it is not the last expression in
the body.
:::

### Exercises

2. Write `event_rate_or()`, which takes `data`, `site_name`, and a
   third argument `default` with no default value of its own set
   in the signature, and returns `event_rate_or()`'s usual
   computation when the site has rows, or `default` when it does
   not. Call it once supplying `default = NA_real_` and once with no
   third argument at all, and explain the second call's error in
   terms of lazy evaluation.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
event_rate_or <- function(data, site_name, default) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  if (nrow(site_data) == 0) return(default)
  mean(site_data$event_30d, na.rm = TRUE)
}
event_rate_or(hf_events, "nonexistent site", default = NA_real_)
#> [1] NA
event_rate_or(hf_events, "nonexistent site")
#> Error in `event_rate_or()`:
#> ! argument "default" is missing, with no default
```
:::


`default` has no default value, so it is a promise with nothing to
evaluate. The promise is never forced on the first call, because
`site_name` matches and `return(default)` is never reached. On the
second call the site is missing, so `return(default)` is reached.
R then tries to evaluate the promise for `default`. It finds no
value and no expression to compute it from, and raises 'argument
"default" is missing, with no default'. In other words, under lazy
evaluation an unsupplied argument with no default is not an error
until the moment it is actually needed.
:::

## Scoping and closures {#sec-functions-scoping}

Suppose a function uses a name that it does not define as an
argument or a local variable. R looks up that name in the
environment where the function was *created*, not the environment
where it is *called*. This is lexical scoping. A function together
with the environment it remembers from its creation is a
**closure**. Lexical scoping has visible consequences once a
function returns another function, which is how a *function
factory* works. `make_rate_fn()` below takes a data frame and
returns a function. The returned function computes a site's event
rate against that specific data frame, even though `data` does not
appear in its own argument list:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_rate_fn <- function(data) {
  function(site_name) {
    site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
    mean(site_data$event_30d, na.rm = TRUE)
  }
}

rate_all_arms <- make_rate_fn(hf_events)
hf_events_uc <- filter(hf_events, arm == "Usual care")
rate_usual_care <- make_rate_fn(hf_events_uc)

c(all_arms = rate_all_arms("Site A"),
  usual_care_only = rate_usual_care("Site A"))
#>        all_arms usual_care_only 
#>        0.206422        0.218845
```
:::


Each call to `make_rate_fn()` creates a fresh execution environment
that holds its own `data`. The function it returns carries that
environment with it, wherever it is called from next. For this
reason `rate_all_arms()` and `rate_usual_care()` disagree about
Site A, although neither takes a `data` argument that could be
confused with the other's. The binding is also frozen at the moment
`make_rate_fn()` evaluated its argument. It is not tied to whatever
the name `hf_events` happens to point to later:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
hf_events_full <- hf_events
hf_events <- filter(hf_events, FALSE)   # pretend it got emptied
rate_all_arms("Site A")                 # unaffected
#> [1] 0.206422
hf_events <- hf_events_full             # later chunks need the data
```
:::


`rate_all_arms()` still reports the original rate. Reassigning
`hf_events` in the global environment changes what that *name*
points to. It does not change the value already captured inside
`rate_all_arms()`'s own enclosing environment. On the one hand,
this is reassuring when you want it. A report built from functions
created earlier in a session is not altered after the fact by a
later, unrelated reassignment. On the other hand, it is confusing
when you do not expect it. A function you believe uses 'the current
cleaned data' may in fact be using a snapshot from whenever it was
created, and `source()`-ing the cleaning step again does not update
it. The practical consequence [@wickham2019advr, ch. 7] is to treat
a closure's captured data as a value fixed at creation. Whenever
the data it closed over changes, rebuild the closure; rerunning the
script around it is not enough.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** `counter <- local({ n <- 0; function() { n <<- n + 1; n } })`
creates a function with no arguments. Calling `counter()` three
times in a row returns `1`, `2`, `3`. Where does the state `n` live
between calls, given that `counter()` has no arguments and no
global variable named `n` is visible at the top level?

**Answer.** `n` lives in `counter`'s enclosing environment. That
environment was created once by `local()` and captured when the
function was defined. `<<-` (superassignment) modifies `n` in that
enclosing environment rather than creating a local copy inside the
call. Each call therefore sees and updates the same `n` that the
previous call left behind. `ls(environment(counter))` shows `n`
there. It is invisible from the top level because `local()` did not
expose any of the names created inside it.
:::

### Exercises

3. Write `make_threshold_flagger(cutoff)`, returning a function
   that takes a numeric vector and returns `TRUE`/`FALSE` for values
   above `cutoff`. Create `flag_high_bnp <- make_threshold_flagger(1000)`
   and `flag_very_high_bnp <- make_threshold_flagger(5000)`, and
   show that changing `cutoff` in your own session afterward does
   not change either function's behavior.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_threshold_flagger <- function(cutoff) {
  function(x) x > cutoff
}
flag_high_bnp <- make_threshold_flagger(1000)
flag_very_high_bnp <- make_threshold_flagger(5000)
bnp <- c(200, 1200, 6000)

cutoff <- 0   # a later, unrelated reassignment of the same name
rbind(high = flag_high_bnp(bnp), very_high = flag_very_high_bnp(bnp))
#>            [,1]  [,2] [,3]
#> high      FALSE  TRUE TRUE
#> very_high FALSE FALSE TRUE
```
:::


Each call to `make_threshold_flagger()` created its own execution
environment, with its own binding for `cutoff`. The function it
returned captured that binding. The later line `cutoff <- 0`
creates or changes a binding in the *global* environment. Neither
returned function looks there. Each one looks up `cutoff` in the
environment where it was defined, not in the caller's environment.
:::

## Iteration: map over for {#sec-functions-iteration}

The bug in the opening example becomes visible once the loop is
written in two ways. The first version loops over site labels taken
from last week's report. As @sec-types established, those labels
mix the canonical `"Site A"` with casing and whitespace variants of
the other four. The loop assigns each result into a list with
`[[<-`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
site_labels <- c("Site A", "site b", "SITE C", " Site D", "Site E ")

for_result <- list()
for (i in seq_along(site_labels)) {
  for_result[[i]] <- site_event_rate(hf_events, site_labels[i])
}
length(for_result)
#> [1] 1
for_result
#> [[1]]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   700      0.206
```
:::


Four of the five labels do not exactly match a value in
`hf_rand$site`, so `site_event_rate()` returns `NULL` for each.
Assigning `NULL` to an element of a list with `result[[i]] <- NULL`
does not store a `NULL`. Instead, it *deletes that element*, and
every later index shifts down. The loop above runs five times, and
the list it builds has length 1. There is no
error and no warning, because each step, taken alone, is legal R.
`purrr::map()` behaves differently on the same inputs:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(purrr)

map_result <- map(site_labels, site_event_rate, data = hf_events)
names(map_result) <- site_labels
map_result
#> $`Site A`
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   700      0.206
#> 
#> $`site b`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`SITE C`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $` Site D`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`Site E `
#> NULL
```
:::


`map()` always returns a list the same length as its input, with
one element per call. A `NULL` result is stored as a `NULL`
*element*. It is visible at its own position, with the label that
produced it still attached. Of the two results, only the length-5
list with four visible `NULL`s shows you that there is a problem,
and where. `sapply()` sits between the two, and its behavior
depends on what it gets back. When the results are not all the
same type and length, as here, `simplify = TRUE` fails silently and
`sapply()` returns a list, as `map()` does. When the results would
simplify, `sapply()` returns a vector or matrix instead of a list.
That is, the type of what you get back depends on data you have
not yet seen. `map()` always returns a list, whatever the input.

@tbl-functions-iteration-compare summarizes the three.

| | `for` (`result[[i]] <- f(x[i])`) | `sapply()` | `purrr::map()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length of result | Can shrink if `f()` returns `NULL` | Can shrink the same way inside its own loop | Always equals `length(x)` |
| Return type | Whatever you built | Vector, matrix, or list, decided after the fact | Always a list |
| On an error | Stops the whole loop immediately | Stops the whole call immediately | Stops, unless wrapped (below) |

: Three ways to iterate a function over a vector, and what each
guarantees about what comes back. {#tbl-functions-iteration-compare}

A second hazard appears once the function can raise an error
rather than quietly return `NULL`. The stricter version below
refuses an unmatched site instead of returning nothing:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
site_event_rate_strict <- function(data, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  if (nrow(site_data) == 0) {
    stop("no rows found for site '", site_name, "'")
  }
  summarize(site_data, n = n(),
            event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
}
```
:::


A `for` loop over the same five labels stops entirely at the first
failure, having processed only the sites before it:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
for_strict <- list()
for (i in seq_along(site_labels)) {
  for_strict[[i]] <- site_event_rate_strict(hf_events, site_labels[i])
}
#> Error in `site_event_rate_strict()`:
#> ! no rows found for site 'site b'
```
:::


`purrr::possibly()` wraps a function so that an error is caught and
replaced with a stand-in value. The iteration then continues
through every element:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
safe_rate <- possibly(site_event_rate_strict, otherwise = NA)
safe_result <- map(site_labels, safe_rate, data = hf_events)
names(safe_result) <- site_labels
safe_result
#> $`Site A`
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   700      0.206
#> 
#> $`site b`
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $`SITE C`
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $` Site D`
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $`Site E `
#> [1] NA
```
:::


`purrr::safely()` is the same idea with nothing discarded. Instead
of a stand-in value, it returns a list with `result` and `error`
for each element. A later step can then see exactly which calls
failed and why, not only that they did. Use `possibly()` when a
stand-in value is an acceptable answer (a missing site becomes
`NA`, dropped from a later `mean()`). Use `safely()` when you need
to inspect or report the failures themselves, for example to tell a
teammate which sites to investigate before rerunning anything.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that `possibly()` catches errors per element, not all or
nothing. Count how many of the five calls failed and how many
succeeded:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
outcomes <- map_lgl(safe_result, ~ !identical(.x, NA))
c(succeeded = sum(outcomes), failed = sum(!outcomes))
#> succeeded    failed 
#>         1         4
```
:::


One call (the exact match, `"Site A"`) succeeds and four fail.
This matches the four casing and whitespace mismatches in
`site_labels`. A `for` loop over the strict function would have
told you only that *something*, at or before the second element,
failed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does the `for`-loop version earlier in this
section end up with a list of length 1 rather than, say, length 4
with the `NULL`s simply missing from wherever they would have gone?

**Answer.** `result[[i]] <- NULL` does not skip an assignment. It
removes element `i` if one exists, and inserts nothing if it does
not. The list therefore never grows past the last *successful*
assignment. Here only the first of five iterations (`"Site A"`)
succeeds, so the list has exactly one element. The second iteration
deletes the nonexistent second element, which does nothing, and so
do the third through fifth. The resulting length tells you nothing
about which four sites were skipped. By contrast, `map()`'s
length-5 list shows the failures by position.
:::

   that it has the same length guarantee as `map()`: preallocate the
   result list and assign by name rather than by
   `[[<-`-ing a possibly-`NULL` value into a growing list.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
for_fixed <- vector("list", length(site_labels))
names(for_fixed) <- site_labels
for (i in seq_along(site_labels)) {
  for_fixed[site_labels[i]] <- list(site_event_rate(hf_events, site_labels[i]))
}
length(for_fixed)
#> [1] 5
for_fixed
#> $`Site A`
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n event_rate
#>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1   700      0.206
#> 
#> $`site b`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`SITE C`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $` Site D`
#> NULL
#> 
#> $`Site E `
#> NULL
```
:::


`vector("list", n)` preallocates a length-`n` list of `NULL`s.
`for_fixed[site_labels[i]] <- list(...)` uses single-bracket
assignment with a one-element list on the right. This replaces an
element in place rather than deleting it. The preallocation now
guarantees the length, whatever any call returns. We note that the
fix does not remove the underlying bug (the mismatched labels). It
only stops a second bug (the shrinking list) from hiding the first
one.
:::

5. Using `map_dbl()` instead of `map()`, compute the event rate
   (not a summary data frame) for every HF-HOME site using the
   correct, canonical labels, and explain why `map_dbl()` is a
   better choice than `map()` here if you intend to pass the result
   straight into `ggplot2`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
canonical_sites <- sort(unique(hf_rand$site))
rates <- map_dbl(canonical_sites, function(s) {
  mean(filter(hf_events, site == s)$event_30d, na.rm = TRUE)
})
names(rates) <- canonical_sites
rates
#>    Site A    Site B    Site C    Site D    Site E 
#> 0.2064220 0.2462687 0.2121212 0.2464183 0.2126866
```
:::


`map_dbl()` requires every call to return a length-one numeric
value. It fails loudly at the first call that does not. `map()`
would instead return a list, which would have to be converted
before a plotting function could use it. For a result bound for a
numeric column, the extra constraint turns a type mismatch into an
error at the point it happens. Without it, the mismatch would
surface as a confusing message three steps later inside `ggplot2`.
:::

## Debugging your own code {#sec-functions-debugging}

The tools in this section assume an interactive R session. A book
rendered in one batch process cannot pause for you. Each tool is
therefore shown as a console transcript rather than an executed
chunk, except where the condition can be reproduced and captured
without a pause. Read each transcript as what you would see if you
typed the same lines at your own prompt, immediately after the
error it follows.

**`traceback()`: after the fact.** When an uncaught error stops a
top-level command, R keeps the sequence of calls that led to it
until the next command runs. `traceback()` prints that sequence,
most recent call first. It tells you which function in the chain
actually called `stop()`, and which functions merely called *it*:

```r
> site_event_rate_strict(hf_events, "site b")
Error in site_event_rate_strict(hf_events, "site b") :
  no rows found for site 'site b'
> traceback()
1: site_event_rate_strict(hf_events, "site b")
```

For a one-level call like this one, `traceback()` adds little. Its
value grows with the depth of the call stack. Suppose `map()` calls
`site_event_rate_strict()` directly over the labels from
@sec-functions-iteration, without the `possibly()` wrapper. The
failure is then raised several frames down, and the output is:

```r
> map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events)
Error in site_event_rate_strict(data = hf_events, dots[[1L]][[2L]]) :
  no rows found for site 'site b'
> traceback()
4: site_event_rate_strict(data = hf_events, dots[[1L]][[2L]])
3: .f(.x[[i]], ...)
2: map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events)
1: (function() map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events))()
```

Frame 4, the one at the top, is where the error was actually
raised. Everything below it records who called whom to get there.
Read a `traceback()` from the top down, and stop at the first frame
that is your own code and not a library internal. That is almost
always the frame whose assumption was violated.

**`browser()`: a breakpoint you write into the body.** Insert
`browser()` as a line inside a function. The next time the function
runs, execution pauses there. You are placed at an interactive
prompt with that call's local variables in scope:

```r
site_event_rate <- function(data, site_name) {
  site_data <- filter(data, site == site_name)
  browser()
  if (nrow(site_data) > 0) {
    summarize(site_data, n = n(), event_rate = mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE))
  }
}
site_event_rate(hf_events, "site b")
Called from: site_event_rate(hf_events, "site b")
Browse[1]> nrow(site_data)
[1] 0
Browse[1]> site_name
[1] "site b"
Browse[1]> unique(data$site)
[1] "Site A" "Site B" "Site C" "Site D" "Site E"
Browse[1]> c
```

The `Browse[1]>` prompt accepts ordinary R code, evaluated in the
function's own execution environment. It also accepts a few
one-letter commands. `n` steps to the next line, `c` continues to
completion (or the next `browser()`), and `Q` aborts back to the
top level. Here `nrow(site_data)` is `0`, and `unique(data$site)`
does not contain `"site b"`. That is the bug, seen directly rather
than inferred from a stack trace. Remove the `browser()` line once
you are done. It is easy to leave one in a committed file by
accident, and a reviewer who hits it has no idea why the session
froze.

**`debugonce()`: the same pause, with nothing left behind.**
`debugonce(f)` sets a breakpoint at the start of `f()` for exactly
its *next* call, then removes itself. You never edit the function's
source to insert or delete a `browser()` line:

```r
> debugonce(site_event_rate)
> site_event_rate(hf_events, "site b")
debugging in: site_event_rate(hf_events, "site b")
Browse[2]> n
Browse[2]> n
Browse[2]> nrow(site_data)
[1] 0
```

Each `n` steps one line further into the function body and stops
before that line executes. This is the natural tool when you want
to watch a function's state change statement by statement, rather
than jump straight to one line. `debug(f)` is the same idea without
the 'once'. It stays armed until you call `undebug(f)`. That is
useful while you are actively working on a function, but it is easy
to forget and leave armed afterward.

**`options(error = recover)`: a menu instead of a single pause.**
Set globally, it intercepts *every* uncaught error in the session
and offers a menu of frames to enter. You do not need to predict
which function will fail and instrument it in advance:

```r
> options(error = recover)
> map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events)
Error in site_event_rate_strict(data = hf_events, dots[[1L]][[2L]]) :
  no rows found for site 'site b'

Enter a frame number, or 0 to exit

1: map(site_labels, site_event_rate_strict, data = hf_events)
2: .f(.x[[i]], ...)
3: site_event_rate_strict(data = hf_events, dots[[1L]][[2L]])

Selection: 3
Called from: eval(expr, p)
Browse[1]> site_name
[1] "site b"
```

It is the right tool when you do not yet know which function is at
fault, which describes most real debugging. `browser()` and
`debugonce()` are the right tools once you already suspect one.
Reset it with `options(error = NULL)` when you are done. Otherwise
it stays armed for the rest of the session and surprises the next
person who sees your `.Rprofile`.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
An agent can narrow where to look before you open the debugger
yourself.

> **Context.** `site_event_rate()`, defined in this session, returns
> a data frame for a site that matches rows and `NULL` otherwise.
> Called in a loop over `c("Site A", "site b", "SITE C", " Site D", "Site E ")`
> against `hf_events`, it should produce five rows, one per site.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not modify `site_event_rate()`. Investigate
> only by running read-only R code (inspecting values, not editing
> files) in this session.
>
> **Criteria.** For each of the five labels, report whether
> `filter(hf_events, site == label)` returns zero rows or more than
> zero, and if zero, show the exact character-by-character
> difference between that label and the value in
> `unique(hf_events$site)` it was meant to match.

*Failure mode.* An agent asked to 'fix the bug' might instead edit
`filter()` to match case-insensitively and call it done. That
repairs this one symptom. The underlying problem, that two
different tables disagree on how to write a site name, is left
undiagnosed and undocumented. *Check.* Confirm that the agent's
report names all four mismatches (casing on two, leading or
trailing whitespace on two) rather than stopping at the first one.
Also confirm that it changed no file. The fix belongs in a decision
about which table is the source of truth for site labels, not in a
case-insensitive patch.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You set `options(error = recover)`, trigger an error,
and the menu lists five frames. Which one should you enter first?

**Answer.** Usually the deepest frame that is still your own code,
not a library internal. The error is raised at the bottom of the
list (the most recently called function). However, the state most
useful to inspect is often one or two frames up. That is the point
where your code called into a library function with an argument
that was already wrong. Entering the exact frame that called
`stop()` tells you what failed. Entering the frame above it often
tells you why.
:::

6. Using `browser()`, find why `clean_sbp()` below returns `-99` for
   one value instead of `NA`. (Hint: the condition compares a
   trimmed string against an untrimmed one.)


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean_sbp <- function(x) {
  trimmed <- trimws(x)
  x[trimmed == "-99 "] <- NA
  as.numeric(x)
}
clean_sbp(c("120", "-99 ", "-99"))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Insert `browser()` after the `trimmed <- trimws(x)` line and inspect
`trimmed`. It is `c("120", "-99", "-99")`. Trimming removed the
trailing space, so `trimmed == "-99 "` (with a trailing space in
the pattern) matches neither element. The fix compares like with
like:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean_sbp <- function(x) {
  trimmed <- trimws(x)
  trimmed[trimmed == "-99"] <- NA
  as.numeric(trimmed)
}
clean_sbp(c("120", "-99 ", "-99"))
#> [1] 120  NA  NA
```
:::


In the original, `-99` silently survived as a numeric value, and
nothing marked it as different from a real low blood pressure.
This is the quiet, plausible-looking failure that Habit 8 warns
about.
:::

## Clear errors and warnings {#sec-functions-errors}

`base::stop()` raises a condition of class `"simpleError"` carrying
only a character message. `rlang::abort()` raises the same kind of
condition, but it lets you attach a custom class and arbitrary
data. The error is then not only something a human reads. Code
downstream can also catch it and act on it. `check_stratum()` below
validates `ef_stratum` against the HF-HOME codebook. On failure, it
reports the unrecognized values as structured data, not only as
text embedded in a message:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(rlang)

check_stratum <- function(x) {
  valid <- c("Reduced EF", "Preserved EF")
  bad <- setdiff(unique(x), valid)
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    abort(
      message = paste0("unrecognized ef_stratum value(s): ",
                       paste(bad, collapse = ", ")),
      class = "hf_bad_stratum",
      bad_values = bad
    )
  }
  invisible(x)
}

check_stratum(hf_rand$ef_stratum)   # the real column: passes silently
```
:::


A corrupted copy, with one stratum written in lower case, triggers
the error. Catching it by class, rather than by parsing the
message, recovers the exact offending values as data:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
corrupted <- c(hf_rand$ef_stratum, "reduced ef")
caught <- tryCatch(
  check_stratum(corrupted),
  hf_bad_stratum = function(e) e
)
class(caught)
#> [1] "hf_bad_stratum" "rlang_error"    "error"          "condition"
caught$bad_values
#> [1] "reduced ef"
```
:::


The base equivalent is possible but takes more work. `stop()` takes
only text. To catch a specific kind of error other than by matching
a substring of the message, you must wrap the condition yourself
with `structure(class = c("hf_bad_stratum", "error",
"condition"), ...)`. `abort()` does this for you, correctly, every
time. A caller that wants to catch only `hf_bad_stratum` errors,
and let every other error propagate, writes `tryCatch(expr,
hf_bad_stratum = handler)`. Matching on a message substring instead
breaks as soon as the wording changes. That is the kind of brittle
test @sec-testing-smells warns against, now in production code
rather than a test file.

**What `rlang::last_trace()` adds.** `traceback()` shows the raw
call stack. `rlang::last_trace()`, called after an error raised by
`abort()`, shows the same information as a tree of nested calls.
The condition object it stores also keeps `abort()`'s data payload
accessible:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
check_stratum(corrupted)
#> Error in `check_stratum()`:
#> ! unrecognized ef_stratum value(s): reduced ef
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
last_trace()
#> <error/hf_bad_stratum>
#> Error in `check_stratum()`:
#> ! unrecognized ef_stratum value(s): reduced ef
#> ---
#> Backtrace:
#>     x
#>  1. \-global check_stratum(corrupted)
#> Run rlang::last_trace(drop = FALSE) to see 1 hidden frame.
```
:::


The indentation in `last_trace()`'s output shows which call was
made from inside which other call. This matters once a validation
helper like `check_stratum()` is itself called from inside a
cleaning pipeline several layers deep. `traceback()`'s flat list,
most recent first, carries the same information. However, it leaves
you to reconstruct the nesting yourself, without any indentation to
guide you.

This is Habit 8 applied in code. If nothing asserts what the valid
values are, a quietly miscoded stratum value will not stop the
pipeline. The pipeline will continue to a plausible but wrong
summary. `check_stratum()` is the assertion that makes that quiet
failure loud. The error also carries enough structure (`bad_values`,
a specific `class`) for a caller to decide automatically whether to
stop, warn, or drop the offending rows. It is not limited to
printing a message for a human to read.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A caught error you do not re-raise or log has simply vanished.**
`tryCatch(risky_step(), error = function(e) NULL)` makes a failure
disappear as completely as the `NULL`-returning function at the
start of this chapter did. The only difference is that it does so
on purpose. Catch an error only when you have a specific recovery
in mind for it (a default value, a retry, a skip with a recorded
reason). Otherwise let it propagate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** `abort()`'s `class` argument accepts a character
vector, not just one string, for example `class = c("hf_bad_stratum", "hf_validation_error")`.
What does giving it two classes let a caller do that one class does
not?

**Answer.** A `tryCatch()` handler matches on any class a condition
has. A caller interested in HF-HOME validation errors in general
can catch `hf_validation_error`. It can then handle every specific
kind of validation failure (bad stratum, bad sex code, bad date)
the same way. A caller that cares specifically about the stratum
problem can still catch `hf_bad_stratum` alone. With one string,
every caller must know the exact, specific class. A small hierarchy
lets callers choose how broadly to catch.
:::

### Exercises

7. Rewrite `check_stratum()`'s base-R equivalent using `stop()` and
   `structure()` so that a caller can still catch it by class as
   `"hf_bad_stratum"`, without using `rlang`. Compare the line count
   with the `abort()` version.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
check_stratum_base <- function(x) {
  valid <- c("Reduced EF", "Preserved EF")
  bad <- setdiff(unique(x), valid)
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    cond <- structure(
      class = c("hf_bad_stratum", "error", "condition"),
      list(message = paste0("unrecognized ef_stratum value(s): ",
                            paste(bad, collapse = ", ")),
           call = sys.call(-1), bad_values = bad)
    )
    stop(cond)
  }
  invisible(x)
}
caught_base <- tryCatch(check_stratum_base(corrupted),
                        hf_bad_stratum = function(e) e)
caught_base$bad_values
#> [1] "reduced ef"
```
:::


The base version does the same job in roughly the same number of
lines. However, each piece is a detail that `abort()` supplies by
default: the three-element class vector, and the `message` and
`call` fields a condition object must have. Each detail is also a
place to get the base version subtly wrong. For example, leaving
`"condition"` out of the class vector breaks `tryCatch()`
entirely, and silently, until someone tries to catch it.
:::

## Testing functions in isolation {#sec-functions-testing}

Every function in this chapter has been called directly, on a
data frame built for the purpose, and not only inside the pipeline
that would normally call it. `site_event_rate_strict()`, for
example, has been run with the full `hf_events` table, with a
vector of mismatched labels, and, below, with a four-row fixture
built by hand. @sec-testing-unit makes the argument at length. In
brief, a function is far easier to get right, and to debug when it
is wrong, when its tests call it directly with inputs you chose.
It is much harder when the only evidence of its behavior is
whatever the full pipeline happens to produce from this week's
data.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tinytest)

fixture <- data.frame(
  site = c("Site A", "Site A", "Site B"),
  event_30d = c(1, 0, NA)
)
out <- site_event_rate_strict(fixture, "Site A")
expect_equal(out$n, 2, info = "both Site A rows counted")
#> ----- PASSED      : <-->
#>  call| expect_equal(out$n, 2, info = "both Site A rows counted")
#>  info| both Site A rows counted
expect_equal(out$event_rate, 0.5, info = "one of two ascertained events")
#> ----- PASSED      : <-->
#>  call| expect_equal(out$event_rate, 0.5, info = "one of two ascertained events")
#>  info| one of two ascertained events
expect_error(site_event_rate_strict(fixture, "Site Z"),
             pattern = "no rows found",
             info = "a site absent from the fixture errors, not NULL")
#> ----- PASSED      : <-->
#>  call| expect_error(site_event_rate_strict(fixture, "Site Z"), pattern = "no rows found", 
#>  call| info = "a site absent from the fixture errors, not NULL")
#>  info| a site absent from the fixture errors, not NULL
```
:::


The third assertion is the one that this chapter's opening bug
lacked. It passes against the *strict* version. Run against the
original `site_event_rate()`, which returns `NULL` instead, it
would have failed as soon as someone wrote it. That would have been
long before the function reached a loop over five site labels
copied from the wrong table. Writing the test needs only the
function and a few rows built to exercise exactly the branch in
question. No pipeline, join, or file on disk is needed. Isolate the
function from everything around it before you decide whether it is
correct. Then let the integration layer of
@sec-testing-correctness confirm that the isolated pieces still
work correctly once they are wired together.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The fixture above has `event_30d = NA` for one row
and the test checks `event_rate == 0.5`. Does this test the
function's handling of missing outcomes, or only its handling of
complete ones?

**Answer.** It tests the handling of missing outcomes directly.
`mean(c(1, 0, NA), na.rm = TRUE)` is `0.5`, computed from the two
non-missing rows. The assertion therefore passes only if
`na.rm = TRUE` is actually in effect inside the function. Deleting
`na.rm = TRUE` from `site_event_rate_strict()` would make this
fixture return `NA` for `event_rate`, and the test would fail. A
fixture built only from complete rows would pass either way.
:::

`expect_silent()` is the right assertion for 'raises no error'.
`expect_true(TRUE)` after a bare call is not. `expect_silent()`
fails if the call produces an error, a warning, or even a message.
That is closer to the actual claim ('the real column is clean')
than merely confirming that the function returned.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **A function is one place to fix a bug.** Write a function the
   first time a computation would otherwise be copied, not the
   third. The cost of writing it is small. The cost of finding four
   copies of a bug later is not.
2. **A closure freezes a snapshot, not a live reference.** If a
   function factory's returned function seems to be using stale
   data, suspect that the data it closed over changed after the
   closure was created, not that the closure is reading something
   live.
3. **`map()` over `for` or `sapply()` when the length or type of the
   result matters.** `map()` always returns a list the same length
   as its input. A `for` loop assigning a possibly-`NULL` value
   with `[[<-` can silently shrink. `sapply()`'s return type
   depends on what the calls happen to return.
4. **Habit 8: make the quiet failure loud.** A function that returns
   `NULL`, or a mean computed over the wrong rows, produces a
   plausible-looking answer with no error. `rlang::abort()` with a
   class and a data payload turns a violated assumption into a
   condition that code can catch, not only a message a human might
   miss.
5. **Test a function directly before trusting what the pipeline
   says about it.** A fixture built by hand, with the one edge case
   you are worried about, can find a bug in minutes. The full
   pipeline, run on this week's data, might never exercise that
   case at all.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Define a function with a default | `f <- function(x, y = 1) x + y` | Repeating an argument's usual value at every call site |
| Forward extra arguments | `f <- function(x, ...) g(x, ...)` | Re-naming every option a wrapped function accepts |
| Return early | `if (bad) return(NA)` | An implicit `NULL` from a conditional with no `else` |
| Make a closure | `function(data) function(x) ...` | A function needing a global variable it should not depend on |
| Inspect a closure's captured value | `environment(f)$data` | Assuming a closure reads a name 'live' |
| Iterate, preserving length and type | `purrr::map(x, f)` | A `for` loop or `sapply()` silently shrinking or changing type |
| Iterate numeric results | `purrr::map_dbl(x, f)` | A list where a numeric vector was expected |
| Catch errors per element | `purrr::possibly(f, otherwise = NA)` | A `for` loop stopping at the first failure |
| Catch errors, keep the reason | `purrr::safely(f)` | Losing which inputs failed and why |
| See the call stack after an error | `traceback()` | Guessing which function actually failed |
| Pause inside a function, every call | `browser()` inside the body | Not knowing what to add until you see the state |
| Pause once, no file edit | `debugonce(f)` | A `browser()` call left behind in committed code |
| Pause at the first uncaught error, any function | `options(error = recover)` | Having to guess which function to instrument first |
| Raise a catchable, data-carrying error | `rlang::abort(msg, class = "...", data = ...)` | A `stop()` message a caller can only parse as text |
| See a readable, nested call tree | `rlang::last_trace()` | Reconstructing nesting from a flat `traceback()` |
| Test one function, not the pipeline | A hand-built fixture plus `tinytest::expect_*()` | A bug the full pipeline happens not to exercise |

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-14b}

1. The value of the last expression evaluated in the function's
   body, whether or not that expression is the last line written.
   A conditional with no matching branch, for instance, evaluates
   to `NULL`. That `NULL` is what the function returns, even though
   no line in it says `return(NULL)`.
2. `purrr::map()` stores each call's result as an element of a
   list whose length is fixed in advance. A `NULL` result therefore
   occupies its own visible position rather than being omitted. A
   `for` loop that assigns with `result[[i]] <- f(x[i])` uses
   `[[<-` assignment. Under `[[<-`, assigning `NULL` *deletes* that
   list element instead of storing it. The loop can therefore
   finish with a shorter list than the number of iterations it ran.
3. `rlang::abort()` lets an error carry a custom class and
   arbitrary named data. The class lets a caller catch exactly that
   kind of failure with `tryCatch()`, rather than parsing the
   message text. The data let the caller recover structured
   information about what went wrong, such as which values were
   invalid, rather than only a human-readable sentence. The purpose
   is to turn a violated assumption into something code downstream
   can act on automatically, not only something a person reading
   the console can react to.
